{{short description|Electromagnetic geophysical technique}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2026}}
[[File:LEMI405.jpg|thumb|Magnetotelluric station]]

'''Magnetotellurics''' ('''MT''') is an [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetic]] [[geophysics|geophysical]] method for inferring the [[Earth]]'s subsurface electrical conductivity from measurements of natural geomagnetic and geoelectric field variation at the Earth's surface.

Investigation depth ranges from 100&nbsp;m below ground by recording higher frequencies down to 200&nbsp;km or deeper with long-period soundings. Proposed in Japan in the 1940s, and France and the USSR during the early 1950s, MT is now an international academic discipline and is used in exploration surveys around the world.

Commercial uses include [[hydrocarbon]] (oil and gas) exploration, [[Geothermal energy|geothermal]] exploration, [[carbon sequestration]], mining exploration, as well as [[hydrocarbon]] and [[groundwater]] monitoring. Research applications include experimentation to further develop the MT technique, long-period deep crustal exploration, deep mantle probing, sub-glacial water flow mapping, and earthquake precursor research.

== History ==

The magnetotelluric technique was introduced independently by Japanese scientists in 1948<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rikitake |first1=T. |year=1948 |title=Notes on electromagnetic induction within the Earth. |journal=Bull. Earthq. Res. Inst.  |volume=24 |issue=1 |page=4}}</ref> (Hirayama, Rikitake), [[Soviet]] geophysicist [[Andrey Nikolayevich Tikhonov]] in 1950<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tikhonov |first1=A.N. |year=1950 |title=On determining electrical characteristics of the deep layers of the Earth's crust |journal=Doklady |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=295–297 |id={{NAID|10004593077}} }}</ref> and the French geophysicist Louis Cagniard in 1953.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Cagniard | first1 = L | year = 1953 | title = Basic theory of the magneto-telluric method of geophysical prospecting | journal = Geophysics | volume = 18 | issue = 3| pages = 605–635 | doi=10.1190/1.1437915| bibcode = 1953Geop...18..605C}}</ref> With advances in instrumentation, processing and modelling, magnetotellurics has become one of the most important tools in deep Earth research.

Since first being created in the 1950s, magnetotelluric sensors, receivers and data processing techniques have followed the general trends in electronics, becoming less expensive and more capable with each generation. Major advances in MT instrumentation and technique include the shift from analog to digital hardware, the advent of remote referencing, GPS time-based synchronization, and 3D data acquisition and processing.

== Commercial applications ==

=== Hydrocarbon exploration ===
For [[hydrocarbon exploration]], MT is mainly used as a complement to the primary technique of [[reflection seismology]] exploration.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.hagi.or.id/download/JGeofisika/2004_2/2004_2_3.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=26 November 2009 |archive-date=21 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721121556/http://www.hagi.or.id/download/JGeofisika/2004_2/2004_2_3.pdf |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Unsworth |first1=Martyn |title=New developments in conventional hydrocarbon exploration with electromagnetic methods |journal=CSEG Recorder |date=April 2005 |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=34–38 |url=https://csegrecorder.com/articles/view/new-developments-in-conventional-hydrocarbon-exploration-with-em-methods }}</ref><ref name="autogenerated1">http://scitation.aip.org/getabs/servlet/GetabsServlet?prog=normal&id=LEEDFF000025000004000438000001&idtype=cvips&gifs=yes{{dead link|date=January 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kmstechnologies.com/Files/MT_for_Oil__and_Gas_Exploration_2008_FINAL_10.17.08.pdf |title=Geothermal Exploration with Electromagnetic Methods |access-date=18 October 2011|year=2008}}</ref> While seismic imaging is able to image subsurface structure, it cannot detect the changes in resistivity associated with hydrocarbons and hydrocarbon-bearing formations. MT does detect [[resistivity]] variations in subsurface structures, which can differentiate between structures bearing hydrocarbons and those that do not.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phoenix-geophysics.com/applications/oil_and_gas/ |title=Oil and Gas exploration |publisher=Phoenix-geophysics.com |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref>

At a basic level of interpretation, resistivity is correlated with different rock types. High-velocity layers are typically highly resistive, whereas [[sediments]] – porous and permeable – are typically much less resistive. While high-velocity layers are an acoustic barrier and make seismic ineffective, their electrical resistivity means the magnetic signal passes through almost unimpeded. This allows MT to see deep beneath these acoustic barrier layers, complementing the seismic data and assisting interpretation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Strack |first1=K. -M. |last2=Hoerdt |first2=A. |last3=Wolfgram |first3=P. A. |last4=Vozoff |first4=K. |title=Integrated electromagnetic and seismic methods for petroleum exploration |journal=Exploration Geophysics |date=June 1991 |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=375–378 |doi=10.1071/eg991375 |bibcode=1991ExG....22..375S }}</ref> 3-D MT survey results in Uzbekistan (32 x 32 grid of soundings) have guided further seismic mapping of a large known gas-bearing formation with complex subsurface geology.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phoenix-geophysics.com/news/newsletter/?&issue=47&article=427 |title=3-D MT SURVEY IN UZBEKISTAN |publisher=Phoenix-geophysics.com |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.publish.csiro.au/paper/ASEG2003ab054.htm |title=Exploration for deep Paleozoic sediments in Uzbekistan using MT: Project "Paleorift" |journal=ASEG Extended Abstracts |date=August 2003 |volume=2003 |issue=2 |pages=1–4 |publisher=Publish.csiro.au |access-date=18 October 2011|doi=10.1071/aseg2003ab054 |s2cid=131364985 |doi-access=free |last1=Fox |first1=L. |last2=Ingerov |first2=A. |last3=Abidov |first3=A. A. |last4=Dovgopolov |first4=F. G. |last5=Babajanov |first5=T. L. |last6=Basov |first6=M. D. |last7=Kocherov |first7=A. B. |last8=Feldman |first8=I. S. |last9=Avram |first9=Y. |last10=Finateu |first10=C. |bibcode=2003ASEGA2003ab054F }}</ref>

[[China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC) and [http://www.nw-geophysics.com Nord-West Ltd] use onshore MT more than any other oil company in the world, conducting thousands of MT soundings for [[hydrocarbon]] exploration and [[map]]ping throughout the globe.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phoenix-geophysics.com/news/newsletter/?&issue=19 |title=SYSTEM 2000 FUELS EXPLORATION BOOM |publisher=Phoenix-geophysics.com |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref>

=== Mining exploration ===

MT is used for various [[base metals]] (e.g. nickel) and [[precious metals]] exploration, as well as for [[kimberlite]] mapping.

[[Vale Inco|INCO]]'s 1991 proof-of-concept study in [[Greater Sudbury|Sudbury]], Ontario, Canada sensed a 1750-meter-deep nickel deposit. [[Falconbridge Ltd.|Falconbridge]] followed with a feasibility study in 1996 that accurately located two Ni-Cu mineralized zones at about 800 m and 1350 m depth. Since then, both major and junior mining companies are increasingly using MT and [[#Audio-magnetotellurics|audio-magnetotellurics]] (AMT) for both brownfields (near known deposits) and greenfields (uncharted land) exploration. Significant MT mapping work has been done on areas of the [[Canadian Shield]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tournerie |first1=Benoit |last2=Chouteau |first2=Michel |title=Analysis of magnetotelluric data along the Lithoprobe seismic line 21 in the Blake River Group, Abitibi, Canada |journal=Earth, Planets and Space |date=May 2002 |volume=54 |issue=5 |pages=575–589 |doi=10.1186/BF03353046 |bibcode=2002EP&S...54..575T |s2cid=54005958 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Diamond exploration, by detecting kimberlites, is also a proven application.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://homepages.dias.ie/~ajones/PowerPoint_Presentations/kimberlite/sld001.htm |title=Imaging the geometry and structure of kimberlite pipes using audio-MT |publisher=Homepages.dias.ie |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref>

=== Geothermal exploration ===

MT [[geothermal exploration]] measurements allow detection of resistivity anomalies associated with productive [[Geothermal activity|geothermal]] structures, including [[fault (geology)|fault]]s and the presence of a [[cap rock]], and allow for estimation of geothermal reservoir temperatures at various depths.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kmstechnologies.com/Files/MT_for_Geothermal_Exploration_2008_FINAL_10.17.08.pdf |title=Geothermal Exploration with Electromagnetic Methods |access-date=18 October 2011|year=2008}}</ref><ref name="kmstechnologies1">{{cite web|url=http://www.kmstechnologies.com/Files/Mapping_geothermal_reservoirs_using_broadband_2-D_MT_and_gravity_data_01.pdf|title=Mapping geothermal reservoirs using broadband 2-D MT and gravity data }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kmstechnologies.com/Files/Characterizing_a_geothermal_reservoir_using_broadband_2-D_MT_survey_01.pdf |title=Characterizing a geothermal reservoir using broadband 2D MT survey in Theistareykir, Iceland |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref> Dozens of MT geothermal exploration surveys have been completed in Japan and the Philippines since the early 1980s, helping to identify several hundred [[megawatts]] of renewable power at places such as the [[Hatchobaru]] plant on [[Kyushu]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.geothermal-energy.org/pdf/IGAstandard/WGC/2005/0718.pdf |title=Magnetotelluric Soundings in the Takigami Geothermal Area, Japan |publisher=International Geothermal Association |access-date=24 January 2018|date=24 April 2005 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://sciencelinks.jp/j-east/article/200512/000020051205A0468633.php |title=Science Links Japan &#124; Geothermal Reservoirs Modeling in the Western Side of Mt. Aso, SW Japan by Magnetotelluric Method |publisher=Sciencelinks.jp |date=18 March 2009 |access-date=18 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120229033055/http://sciencelinks.jp/j-east/article/200512/000020051205A0468633.php |archive-date=29 February 2012 }}</ref> and the Togonang plant on [[Leyte]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.geothermal-energy.org/pdf/IGAstandard/WGC/2005/0611.pdf |title=Resource Potential of the Southern Leyte Geothermal Prospect, Philippines: A Geologic Evaluation |date=24 April 2005 |publisher=International Geothermal Association|author1=Josephine B. Rosell |author2=Maribel C. Zaide-Delfin |access-date=24 January 2018 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pnoc.com.ph/about/milestones.php?page=3 |title=Philippine National Oil Company |publisher=Pnoc.com.ph |access-date=18 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111002074359/http://www.pnoc.com.ph/about/milestones.php?page=3 |archive-date=2 October 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.energy.com.ph/our-projects/geothermal/ |title=Geothermal &#124; The Energy Development Corporation Website |publisher=Energy.com.ph |access-date=18 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151104154602/http://www.energy.com.ph/our-projects/geothermal/ |archive-date=4 November 2015 }}</ref> Geothermal exploration with MT has also been done extensively in [[the United States]], Iceland,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Characterizing a geothermal reservoir using broadband 2-D MT survey in Theistareikir, Iceland|journal=SEG Expanded Abstracts|volume=2008}}</ref> New Zealand, Hungary,<ref name="kmstechnologies1"/> China,<ref>{{dead link|date=June 2019}}http://www.bgp.com.cn/download.aspx?id=156</ref> Ethiopia, Indonesia, Peru,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phoenix-geophysics.com/news/newsletter/?issue=44 |title=Geothermal Mt Survey in Peru |publisher=Phoenix-geophysics.com |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref> Australia, and India.<ref>{{cite journal |id={{INIST|1145977}} |last1=Sinharay |first1=Rajib K |last2=Bhattacharya |first2=Bimalendu B. |title=An analysis of magnetotelluric (MT) data over geothermal region of Bakreshwar, West Bengal |journal=Journal of Geophysics |location=Hyderabad |date=2001 |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=31–39 }}</ref>

===Other===
MT is also used for [[groundwater]] exploration and mapping research, hydrocarbon reservoir monitoring, deep investigation (100&nbsp;km) of the electrical properties of the bedrock for [[high-voltage direct current]] (HVDC) transmission systems,<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1109/PESAFR.2007.4498123 |chapter=Geophysical and geological pre-investigations for HVDC-electrodes |title=2007 IEEE Power Engineering Society Conference and Exposition in Africa - Power ''Africa'' |year=2007 |last1=Thunehed |first1=H. |last2=Astrom |first2=U. |last3=Westman |first3=B. |pages=1–3 |isbn=978-1-4244-1477-2 |s2cid=7541303 }}</ref> [[carbon dioxide]] sequestration,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nrcan-rncan.gc.ca/eneene/science/tirdrdti/clepro-eng.php |title=Energy Sector: Science and Technology: Cleaner Fossil Fuels|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110811170300/http://www.nrcan.gc.ca/eneene/science/tirdrdti/clepro-eng.php|archive-date=11 August 2011 |publisher=Natural Resources Canada |date=4 May 2010 |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phoenix-geophysics.com/news/newsletter/?&issue=43&article=397 |title=MT SURVEY IN TAIWAN EVALUATES THE POSSIBILITY OF CO2 SEQUESTRATION |publisher=Phoenix-geophysics.com |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref> and other environmental engineering applications (e.g. nuclear blast site monitoring<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Unsworth |first1=Martyn |last2=Soyer |first2=Wolfgang |last3=Tuncer |first3=Volkan |last4=Wagner |first4=Anna |last5=Barnes |first5=David |title=Hydrogeologic assessment of the Amchitka Island nuclear test site (Alaska) with magnetotellurics |journal=Geophysics |date=1 May 2007 |volume=72 |issue=3 |pages=B47–B57 |id={{INIST|18787533}} |doi=10.1190/1.2539353 |bibcode=2007Geop...72B..47U |s2cid=2288777 }}</ref> and [[nuclear waste disposal]] site monitoring).

== Research applications ==

===Crust and mantle===

Since the MT is highly sensitive to the composition and temperature of the Earth, it has been widely used to understand numerous geological phenomena in the [[Earth's mantle]] and crust. These include investigating the composition and distribution of [[magma|melts]],<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-018-0217-2|title=Mt St Helens Nature Geoscience Journal Article|journal=Nature Geoscience |date=3 September 2018 |volume=11 |issue=11 |pages=865–870 |doi=10.1038/s41561-018-0217-2 |last1=Bedrosian |first1=Paul A. |last2=Peacock |first2=Jared R. |last3=Bowles-Martinez |first3=Esteban |last4=Schultz |first4=Adam |last5=Hill |first5=Graham J. |s2cid=135191963 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Mid-ocean Ridge Science Journal Article|journal=Science |date=3 March 2017 |volume=355 |issue=6328 |pages=942–945 |doi=10.1126/science.aaj2165 |last1=Sarafian |first1=Emily |last2=Gaetani |first2=Glenn A. |last3=Hauri |first3=Erik H. |last4=Sarafian |first4=Adam R. |s2cid=206653863 |doi-access=free |pmid=28254939 }}</ref> understanding [[fault (geology)|fault mechanics]] and [[earthquake]] generation,<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10712-011-9144-0|title=San Andreas Fault Review Article|journal=Surveys in Geophysics |date=1 December 2011 |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=65–105 |doi=10.1007/s10712-011-9144-0 |last1=Becken |first1=Michael |last2=Ritter |first2=Oliver |s2cid=54882515 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> imaging deep lithospheric architecture and composition, which can be tied to many geodynamic processes.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Southern Africa JGR:SE Journal Article|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |date=12 March 2022 |volume=127 ===Earthquake precursor prediction===

Fluctuations in the MT signal may be able to predict the onset of seismic events.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://tao.cgu.org.tw/index.php?id=380 |title=Terrestrial, Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences |publisher=Tao.cgu.org.tw |date=21 September 1999 |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.tecto.2008.07.019 |title= Short-term earthquake prediction: Current status of seismo-electromagnetics | volume=470 |issue= 3–4 | journal=Tectonophysics |pages=205–213|bibcode=2009Tectp.470..205U |year= 2009 |last1= Uyeda |first1= Seiya |last2= Nagao |first2= Toshiyasu |last3= Kamogawa |first3= Masashi }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tzanis |first1=A. |last2=Vallianatos |first2=F. |title=A critical review of Electric Earthquake Precursors |journal=Annali di Geofisica |volume=44 |issue=2 |date=April 2001 |pages=429–460 |osti=20222530 |hdl=2122/1213 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Stationary MT monitoring systems have been installed in Japan since April 1996, providing a continuous recording of MT signals at the Wakuya Station (previously at the Mizusawa Geodetic Observatory) and the Esashi Station of the [[Geographical Survey Institute of Japan]] (GSIJ).  These stations measure fluctuations in the Earth's [[electromagnetic field]] that correspond with seismic activity.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phoenix-geophysics.com/applications/earthquake_research/short_report_sawauchi.pdf|title=Sawauchi Automated Stationary MT Data and Earthquake Activity (>4.0M) during May ~ August 2008|year=2008}}</ref> The raw geophysical time-series data from these monitoring stations is freely available to the scientific community, enabling further study of the interaction between electromagnetic events and earthquake activity.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://vldb.gsi.go.jp/sokuchi/geomag/menu_03/mt_data-e.html%7B%7Bfull |title=Gsi Home Page - 国土地理院 |access-date=25 February 2010 |archive-date=25 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100225080738/http://vldb.gsi.go.jp/sokuchi/geomag/menu_03/mt_data-e.html%7B%7Bfull |url-status=live }}</ref>

Additional MT earthquake precursor monitoring stations in Japan are located in [[Kagoshima]], in [[Sawauchi]], and on [[Shikoku]]. Similar stations are also deployed in Taiwan on [[Penghu Island]], as well as in the [[Fushan Reserve]] on the island of Taiwan proper.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Chien-Chih |last2=Chen |first2=Chow-Son |last3=Shieh |first3=Chiou-Fen |title=Crustal Electrical Conductors, Crustal Fluids and 1999 Chi-Chi, Taiwan, Earthquake |journal=Terrestrial, Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences |date=2002 |volume=13 |issue=3 |page=367 |doi=10.3319/TAO.2002.13.3.367(CCE) |bibcode=2002TAOS...13..367C |doi-access=free }}</ref>

POLARIS is a Canadian research program investigating the structure and dynamics of the Earth's [[lithosphere]] and the prediction of [[Strong ground motion|earthquake ground motion]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.polarisnet.ca/ |title=Polaris Consortium |publisher=Polarisnet.ca |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref>

==Theory and practice==

===Energy sources===
[[Solar energy]] and [[lightning]] cause natural variations in the [[Earth's magnetic field]], inducing electric currents (known as [[telluric current]]s) under the Earth's surface.<ref>Cantwell, T. (1960) ''Detection and Analysis of Low-Frequency Magnetotelluric Signals'', PhD Thesis, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts</ref>

Different rocks, sediments and geological structures have a wide range of different [[Electrical conductivity|electrical conductivities]].  Measuring electrical resistivity allows different materials and structures to be distinguished from one another and can improve knowledge of [[tectonic]] processes and [[geology|geologic]] structures.

The Earth's naturally varying electric and [[Earth's magnetic field|magnetic fields]] are measured over a wide range of magnetotelluric frequencies from 10,000&nbsp;Hz to 0.0001&nbsp;Hz (10,000&nbsp;s). These fields are due to electric currents flowing in the Earth and the magnetic fields that induce these currents. The magnetic fields are produced mainly by the interaction between the [[solar wind]] and the [[magnetosphere]]. In addition, worldwide [[thunderstorm]] activity causes magnetic fields at frequencies above 1&nbsp;Hz. Combined, these natural phenomena create strong MT source signals over the entire frequency spectrum.

The ratio of the electric field to magnetic field provides simple information about subsurface conductivity. Because the [[skin effect]] phenomenon affects the [[electromagnetic field]]s, the ratio at higher frequency ranges gives information on the shallow Earth, whereas deeper information is provided by the low-frequency range.  The ratio is usually represented as both apparent resistivity as a function of frequency and phase as a function of frequency.

A subsurface [[resistivity]] model is then created using this [[tensor]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://scitation.aip.org/getabs/servlet/GetabsServlet?prog=normal&id=GPYSA7000018000003000605000001&idtype=cvips&gifs=yes&ref=no |title=Basic Theory of the Magneto-Telluric Method of Geophysical Prospecting |journal=Geophysics |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=605–635 |publisher=Scitation.aip.org |access-date=18 October 2011|bibcode=1953Geop...18..605C |last1=Cagniard |first1=Louis |year=1953 |doi=10.1190/1.1437915 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Depth and resolution===
MT measurements can investigate depths from about 300&nbsp;m down to hundreds of kilometers, though investigations in the range of 500&nbsp;m to 10,000&nbsp;m are typical. Greater depth requires measuring lower frequencies, which in turn requires longer recording times. Very deep, very long-period measurements (mid-crust through [[upper mantle (Earth)|upper mantle]] depths), may require recordings of several days to weeks or more to obtain satisfactory data quality.

Horizontal resolution of MT mainly depends on the distance between sounding locations- closer sounding locations increase the horizontal resolution. Continuous profiling (known as Emap) has been used, with only meters between the edges of each telluric dipole.

Vertical resolution of MT mainly depends on the frequency being measured, as lower frequencies have greater depths of penetration. Accordingly, vertical resolution decreases as depth of investigation increases.

===Signal strength and recording times===
Magnetic fields in the frequency range of 1&nbsp;Hz to approximately 20&nbsp;kHz are part of the audio-magnetotelluric (AMT) range.  These are parallel to the Earth surface and move towards the Earth's centre.  This large frequency band allows for a range of depth penetration from several metres to several kilometres below the Earth's surface.  Due to the nature of magnetotelluric source, the waves generally fluctuate in amplitude height.  Long recording times are needed to ascertain usable reading due to the fluctuations and the low signal strength.  Generally, the signal is weak between 1 and 5&nbsp;kHz, which is a crucial range in detecting the top 100&nbsp;m of geology. The magnetotelluric method is also used in marine environments for [[hydrocarbon]] exploration and lithospheric studies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://marineemlab.ucsd.edu/ |title=Marine EM laboratory |publisher=Scripps Institution of Oceanography |date=23 April 2010 |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref> Due to the screening effect of the electrically conductive sea water, a usable upper limit of the spectrum is around 1&nbsp;Hz.

===2D and 3D magnetotellurics===
Two-dimensional surveys consist of a longitudinal profile of MT soundings over the area of interest, providing two-dimensional "slices" of subsurface resistivity.

Three-dimensional surveys consist of a loose grid pattern of MT soundings over the area of interest, providing a more sophisticated three-dimensional model of subsurface resistivity.

== Variants ==

===Audio-magnetotellurics===
Audio-magnetotellurics (AMT) is a higher-frequency magnetotelluric technique for shallower investigations. While AMT has less depth penetration than MT, AMT measurements often take only about one hour to perform (but deep AMT measurements during low-signal strength periods may take up to 24 hours) and use smaller and lighter magnetic sensors. Transient AMT is an AMT variant that records only temporarily during periods of more intense natural signal (transient impulses), improving signal-to-noise-ratio at the expense of strong linear polarization.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.empulse.ca/whatis.html |title=EMpulse Geophysics – Saskatoon |publisher=Empulse.ca |access-date=18 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110827003007/http://www.empulse.ca/whatis.html |archive-date=27 August 2011 }}</ref>

=== Controlled source electromagnetics ===
CSEM [[controlled source electro-magnetic]] is a deep-water [[Offshore (hydrocarbons)|offshore]] variant of controlled source audio magnetotellurics; CSEM is the name used in the offshore oil and gas industry.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://marineemlab.ucsd.edu/resources/concepts/CSEM_MT.html |publisher=Scripps Institution of Oceanography |title= Research &#124; Concepts &#124;CSEM and MT Exploration for Petroleum |date=6 May 2009 |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref> and for onshore exploration mostly Lotem is used in Russia, China the US and Europe<ref>{{Cite book|title=Exploration with Deep Transient Elctromagnetics|last=Strack|first=Kurt|publisher=Elsevier|year=1992|isbn=0-444-89541-8}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Exploration with controlled-source electromagnetics under basalt cover in India|journal=The Leading Edge|volume=26|bibcode=2007LeaEd..26..360S |last1=Strack |first1=K. -M. |last2=Pandey |first2=P. B. |date=2007 |issue=3 |page=360 |doi=10.1190/1.2715056 }}</ref>

Onshore CSEM / CSAMT may be effective where electromagnetic cultural noise (e.g. power lines, electric fences) present interference problems for natural-source geophysical methods.  An extensive grounded wire (2&nbsp;km or more) has currents at a range of frequencies (0.1&nbsp;Hz to 100&nbsp;kHz) passed through it.  The electric field parallel to the source and the magnetic field which is at right angles are measured.  The resistivity is then calculated, and the lower the resistivity, the more likely there is a conductive target (graphite, nickel ore or iron ore). CSAMT is also known in the oil and gas industry as onshore controlled source electromagnetics (Onshore CSEM).

An offshore variant of MT, the marine magnetotelluric (MMT) method,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stéphane |first1=Sainson |title=Electromagnetic seabed logging: a new tool for geoscientists |date=2017 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-45355-2}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=January 2020}} uses instruments and sensors in pressure housings deployed by ship into shallow coastal areas where water is less than 300&nbsp;m deep.<ref name="autogenerated1"/><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://marineemlab.ucsd.edu/resources/Pubs/MarineMTpart1.pdf|title=Marine magnetotellurics for petroleum exploration Part I: A sea-floor equipment system|journal=Geophysics|volume=63|issue=3|pages=816–825|last=Constable|first=Stephen|display-authors=etal|doi=10.1190/1.1444393|bibcode=1998Geop...63..816C|year=1998}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://marineemlab.ucsd.edu/Projects/Gemini/index.html |title=Gemini Prospect Marine MT and CSEM Surveys |publisher=Marineemlab.ucsd.edu |date=6 May 2009 |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phoenix-geophysics.com/news/newsletter/?&issue=34 |title=Marine Mt in China With Phoenix Equipment |publisher=Phoenix-geophysics.com |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.westerngeco.com/services/electromagnetics/mmt.aspx |title=Integrated Electromagnetic Services, WesternGeco |publisher=Westerngeco.com |access-date=18 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091030161422/http://www.westerngeco.com/services/electromagnetics/mmt.aspx |archive-date=30 October 2009 }}</ref> A derivative of MMT is offshore single-channel measurement of the vertical [[magnetic field]] only (the Hz, or "tipper"), which eliminates the need for telluric measurements and horizontal magnetic measurements.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://patentscope.wipo.int/search/en/WO2007079562 |title=CA2006000042 DETECTION OF RESISTIVITY OF OFFSHORE SEISMIC STRUCTURES MAINLY USING VERTICAL MAGNETIC COMPONENT OF EARTH'S NATURALLY VARYING ELECTROMAGNETIC FIELD |publisher=Wipo.int |access-date=25 June 2025}}</ref>

== Exploration surveys ==
MT exploration surveys are done to acquire resistivity data which can be interpreted to create a model of the subsurface. Data is acquired at each sounding location for a period of time (overnight soundings are common), with physical spacing between soundings dependent on the target size and geometry, local terrain constraints and financial cost. Reconnaissance surveys can have spacings of several kilometres, while more detailed work can have 200&nbsp;m spacings, or even adjacent soundings (dipole-to-dipole).

The [[Health, Safety and Environment|HSE]] impact of MT exploration is relatively low because of light-weight equipment, natural signal sources, and reduced hazards compared to other types of exploration (e.g. no drills, no explosives, and no high currents).

=== Remote reference soundings ===
Remote reference is an MT technique used to account for cultural electrical noise by acquiring simultaneous data at more than one MT station. This greatly improves data quality, and may allow acquisition in areas where the natural MT signal is difficult to detect because of man-made [[EM interference]].

=== Equipment ===
A typical full suite of MT equipment (for a "five component" sounding) consists of a receiver instrument with five [[sensors]]:  three [[magnetic]] sensors (typically induction coil sensors), and two [[telluric current|telluric]] (electric) sensors. For exclusively long-period MT (frequencies below approximately 0.1&nbsp;Hz), the three discrete broadband magnetic field sensors may be substituted by a single compact triaxial fluxgate magnetometer. In many situations, only the telluric sensors will be used, and magnetic data borrowed from other nearby soundings to reduce acquisition costs.

A complete five-component set of MT equipment can be backpack-carried by a small field team (2 to 4 persons) or carried by a light [[helicopter]], allowing deployment in remote and rugged areas. Most MT equipment is capable of reliable operation over a wide range of environmental conditions, with ratings of typically −25&nbsp;°C to +55&nbsp;°C, from dry desert to high-humidity (condensing) and temporary full immersion.

=== Data processing and interpretation ===
Post-acquisition processing is required to transform raw time-series data into frequency-based inversions. The resulting output of the processing program is used as the input for subsequent interpretation. Processing may include the use of remote reference data or local data only.

Processed MT data is modelled using various techniques to create a subsurface resistivity map, with lower frequencies generally corresponding to greater depth below ground. Anomalies such as [[fault (geology)|faults]], [[hydrocarbons]], and conductive mineralization appear as areas of higher or lower resistivity from surrounding structures. Various software packages are used for interpretation (inversion) of magnetotelluric data, where apparent resistivity is used to create a model of the subsurface.

== Instrument and sensor manufacturers ==
Four companies supply most of the commercial-use world market:  one in the United States (Zonge International, Inc.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.zonge.com/FieldAMT.html |title=Surveys &#124; AMT and MT |publisher=Zonge |access-date=18 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111003125930/http://www.zonge.com/FieldAMT.html |archive-date=3 October 2011 }}</ref>), one in Canada; (Phoenix Geophysics, Ltd.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phoenix-geophysics.com/products/receivers/mtu/ |title=Phoenix products: The MTU Receiver |publisher=Phoenix-geophysics.com |access-date=18 October 2011}}</ref>); one in Germany (Metronix Messgeraete und Elektronik GmbH).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.geo-metronix.de/ |title=Metronix |publisher=geo-metronix.de}}</ref>) and one in Russia (Vega Geophysics, LLC).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://vega-geo.net/ |title=Vega Geophysics Official Web Site |access-date=28 March 2012}}</ref> Emerging manufacturers of low-cost, internet-enabled long-period and ultrawideband instruments include IoMT in the United States (IoMT LLC).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://iomt.tech/ |title=DART: Hybrid DART systems |publisher=IoMT.tech | access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref>

Government agencies and smaller companies producing MT instrumentation for internal use include the Russian Academy of Sciences (SPbF [[IZMIRAN]]); and the [[Lviv Centre of Institute for Space Research|National Space Research Institute of Ukraine]].
